title: The four triad qualities
summary: Major, minor, diminished, augmented -- four flavors built from two stacked thirds.

steps.title: Two stacked thirds, four flavors
steps.body:
A triad is always built from two thirds stacked on top of each other. Which kind of third you use first, and which one second, decides the chord's character:

- Major  = M3 then m3   ->  1  3  5
- Minor  = m3 then M3   ->  1 b3  5
- Dim.   = m3 then m3   ->  1 b3 b5
- Aug.   = M3 then M3   ->  1  3 #5

That's it. Every triad in every style of music is one of these four.

steps.title: C major triad
steps.body: C E G. The 5-string open C shape: notice the three pitch classes (C, E, G) repeat on different strings.

steps.title: C minor triad
steps.body: C Eb G. Lower the E (string 4 fret 2) by one fret to Eb (fret 1). One single note swap turns happy into sad. Note: this barre voicing is a stretch; the point is to *see* the change, not necessarily to play it cleanly yet.

steps.title: C diminished triad
steps.body: C Eb Gb. Now flat the 5th as well. Diminished sounds tense and unstable -- it almost demands to resolve to another chord.

steps.title: C augmented triad
steps.body: C E G#. Raise the 5th instead. Augmented is symmetrical -- C, E, and G# are all a M3 apart -- which gives it that 'unresolved, floating' quality you hear in jazz turnarounds and movie soundtracks.

steps.title: Ear it out
steps.body: The fastest way to internalize the four qualities is to hear them. Major and minor are easy; diminished is 'the suspense chord'; augmented is 'the dream chord'. The next quiz drills the major/minor 3rd because that's the single interval that flips a triad's identity.
